description_full: Primoris Services Corporation provides infrastructure services primarily in the United States and Canada. The company operates in two segments: Utilities and Energy. The Utilities segment offers installation and maintenance of new and existing natural gas and electric utility distribution and transmission systems, and communications systems. The Energy segment provides engineering, procurement, construction, and maintenance services for entities in the energy, renewable energy and energy storage, renewable fuels, and petroleum and petrochemical industries, as well as state departments of transportation. The company also provides replacement services. Primoris Services Corporation was founded in 1960 and is headquartered in Dallas, Texas.

financial_summary: Primoris Services Corporation is a mid-cap industrials business with a $3.4B market cap on $7.6B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +20% over the past three years and +15% annually across the full decade, the kind of sustained demand persistence that marks a compounder.

Returns on capital run at 12% against a 10% cost of capital, which means the business barely earns its keep economically, and 11% gross margins are typical of commodity economics where competitors can replicate the product cheaply.

The business throws off $340M in free cash flow — roughly 4 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.71× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year, and interest coverage of 19× is fortress-like.

Shareholder yield is only 0.5%, a thin return of capital, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and profit capture is only 0.5× the fair share, suggesting no structural edge inside its industry.

sect: Its 5% operating margin is roughly in line with the Industrials median (9%).
It captures well under its share of sector profits (0.49x its revenue share).
It accounts for 0.2% of sector revenue and 0.1% of sector operating profit.
Over five years it has been gaining share of the sector profit pool (+7.1% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.01 across 544 companies in the universe; the top four hold 9% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a steep downtrend, down 33% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits near the bottom of its 52-week range, 68% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 82% and a beta of 1.18, it moves roughly with the market, though its beta has shifted (1y 0.68 vs 5y 1.29), so read it loosely.
About $95.4M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 58% in the 2020 crash, 41% in the 2022 bear market and 61% in 2008.
val: The stock trades 71% below its DCF fair value of $225, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 47%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $128 to $390 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
Multiples send mixed signals against Industrials peers: cheaper on P/FCF 10.1 vs 22.3, richer on P/E 36.9 vs 23.3 (sector median).
The EBIT multiple is close to its own 10-year median (-7%).
Earnings yields are attractive: an FCF yield of 9.9% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 9.8% (vs the 8% bar).
The 15 covering analysts target $115 on average, 76% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 12% earns above the cost of capital of 9.8%, but the 2pp spread is short of the 7pp moat bar; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.45).
It runs a 11% gross margin and converts 4% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 1.71x.
ROE of 16% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (2.6x equity multiplier).
It spends 0.3% of revenue on stock compensation.
hlth: The balance sheet carries net cash of $65.6M (2% of market cap).
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 3.4, in the safe zone).
Its debt comes due soon (maturity wall about 1.5 years out), so refinancing terms matter.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 19.7% over 3 years, 16.8% over 5 years and 14.7% over 10 years, so growth is accelerating.
At current returns, reinvesting 12% of profits supports about 1.4% a year of fundamental growth, too little to drive meaningful growth.
Free cash flow has compounded 6.6% a year over five years.
Forward indicators: a book-to-bill of 0.87 (orders lagging sales), a backlog worth 70% of annual revenue and deferred revenue up 3%.
Capex roughly matches depreciation (1.4x, 1.7% of sales), a maintenance pace.
Its Rule of 40 score is 21, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders own a modest 1.2%, and reported institutional holdings exceed 100% of shares (a sign of heavy share lending).
Insider trading is two-way: 2 purchases and 9 sales over the past year, net $6.2M sold.
Shareholder yield is a modest 0.5% (0.5% in dividends).
It has paid a dividend for 17 consecutive years, raising it 8.3% a year over the last five.
Short interest is elevated at 12.7% of the float, 3.4 days to cover.
people: With about 18,526 employees, each generates about $409K of revenue, in line with the Industrials median, and productivity has risen 12.5% a year.
That works out to $18K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $1.3M (3x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (3/10, lower is better).
